spec.title: PROP-065 — Structured installation: features, steps, conditions, plan, resume

status.comment: Adopted 2026-10-31 on the owner's request; implemented by the APP-STEPS campaign.

p.purpose: An installer option is an ordered list of steps a reader follows top to bottom: what is fetched, what is built or copied, which command or agent runs, under which condition, with which user-selectable features. The single-method form of `PROP-059#installer-separation` stays as the short spelling of a one-step list. The same declaration is what a planner prints before running, what a graphical editor edits, and what an agent reads to understand an installation without executing it.

p.principle: Everything is data. Steps have a closed set of kinds, conditions have a closed vocabulary, and every step can be answered "will it run, and what does it need" before a byte is downloaded. There is no expression language, no scripting of the installer itself (a script is the content of one step, never the structure), and no transaction: a failed step stops the sequence with its work kept, the index untouched, and a resume point.

p.features: `[[installer_options.features]]` rows (`id`, `name`, optional `description`, `default` boolean) are what a user selects: `--feature ID` / `--no-feature ID` on install, a multi-choice question in an attended terminal when a package declares features and none were named, the defaults unattended. Features change nothing by themselves; steps refer to them through conditions. A feature list may be a tree with relations and named profiles (`#feature-tree`, `#profiles`). The chosen set is recorded with the installation and reused by `update` unless named again.

p.steps: `[[installer_options.steps]]` rows run in file order. Every step has a stable `id`, a human `title`, a `kind`, an optional `description`, optional `when` / `unless` conditions, optional `needs`, an optional `phase` (`prepare`, the default, or `finish`), an optional `optional` boolean, and the fields of its kind. `installation` and `steps` are mutually exclusive in one option; `pre_install` / `post_install` keep working as a leading `prepare` shell step and a leading `finish` shell step respectively.

p.kinds: The kinds are: `env` (`#env-step`); `sources` (fetch, verify and lay out `[[sources]]` as `PROP-059#source-build` does); `archive` (fetch, verify and extract one `zip` / `tar_gz` into `$VIBE_OUT`, with `payload_root`); `recipe` (run a package-relative script under an interpreter in `$VIBE_WORK`); `shell` (run one authored command string under an interpreter, with optional `uninstall`, `force_install`, `force_uninstall`, `update` as today); `native` (run a verified `exe` / `msi` with arguments, Windows only, with the same optional uninstall fields); `copy` (copy package-relative files or directories into `$VIBE_OUT/<destination>`); `agent` (`PROP-064`). A kind outside this list is a manifest error naming the step.

p.result: An option declares what the steps produce: `result = "owned"` (the default when any step writes `$VIBE_OUT`: the non-empty `$VIBE_OUT` is placed as the owned payload, exactly as an archive or a recipe is today) or `result = { external = "<app_root template>" }` (the steps install outside vibe and the root is registered, as a shell or native method is today). Launchers, public commands and portability are per option as before. A `finish` step runs after placement or registration with `VIBE_APP_ROOT` set and the payload as its working directory.

p.conditions: `when` and `unless` take one condition table or an array of them (`when`: all must hold; `unless`: none may hold). The vocabulary is closed: `feature = "ID"`; `param = "ID"`; `param_equals = { id = "ID", value = "V" }`; `command_present = "NAME"` (found on PATH); `file_present = "<template path>"`; `env_present = "NAME"`; `agent_configured = true`; `offline = true`. Every condition is evaluated at planning time from facts the planner already has; a step whose condition is false is reported `skip` with the condition that decided it. No condition reads a file's contents, runs a program or asks a question.

p.needs: `needs` names what a step requires before anything starts: `"network"`, `"command:NAME"`, `"agent"`, `"terminal"`. The planner checks them for every step that will run and refuses the whole installation up front, naming the step and the missing need; `--offline` turns a `network` need of a step without a cache hit into a refusal rather than a late failure. An `optional` step with an unmet need is skipped and reported instead.

p.templates: Step strings that name paths (`file_present`, `copy` destinations, the `external` root, agent prompts) use the one-pass grammar of `PROP-059#launcher-paths` extended with `$work`, `$sources`, `$out`, `$package` and `$feature:ID` (`true` / `false`); `$$` is a literal dollar. A template reference to a secret parameter refuses; secret values remain available through the existing recipe/shell child environment and direct parameter conditions (PROP-069#SECRET-TEMPLATES). Expansion never evaluates a shell. `shell` and `recipe` text is not expanded: it receives the same values as environment variables (`VIBE_WORK`, `VIBE_SOURCES`, `VIBE_OUT`, `VIBE_PACKAGE`, `VIBE_PLATFORM`, `VIBE_ARCH`, `VIBE_APP_ROOT`, and `VIBE_FEATURE_<ID>` / `VIBE_PARAM_<ID>`), so an authored command keeps its own shell syntax.

p.plan: `vibe app plan PACKAGE [selection flags]` resolves the option, the features and every condition and need, and prints the step list as `run` / `skip (reason)` with each step's kind, title, needs and the chosen result, without downloading or running anything (`vibe-app-plan/1` under `--json`). Install, update and project materialisation compute the same plan first and show it before the first step; `--plan-only` on `install` is the same as `plan`. A plan that admits no step producing the declared result is refused. The text form draws the steps as a tree: one node per step carrying its `--from-step` ordinal, its `run` / `skip` word, its `<id> (<kind>)` and its title, each in a column aligned across the whole tree, with its reason and its needs on continuation lines under the label column and each requirement of `#app-dependencies` as a child node of the step that names it. The ordinal stays before the `run` word, where a fixed-width column aligns it whatever the titles do. A requirement an installed version already satisfies says `installed`; one with no such word is installed first, and the plan of that install is headed `plan for <key> (required by <package> for step <id>)` so it is not read as the requiring package's own. The `vibe-app-plan/1` document is unchanged by the tree: a requirement is a `dependency` entry of the requiring plan, and the text is the only tree. The text plan is drawn in the display language of PROP-067: a rule naming the package, its fields as one list, then its steps as a list with their requirements as children (PROP-067 `#heading`, `#list`, `#children`); the document is unchanged.

p.execution: Steps run one at a time in the work directory `<cache>/app-work/<key>/` with `steps.json` (`vibe-app-steps/1`) updated after each step: id, kind, outcome (`done` / `skipped` / `failed` / `delegated`), reason, started and finished times, and for shell / native steps the recorded uninstall data. Output of every child streams live; under `--json` child stdout is relayed to stderr. The work directory is deleted after success unless `--keep-work` is given (`#work`) and after a `finish`-phase failure (the installation is already recorded), and kept after a `prepare`-phase failure or a delegation.

p.resume: `install` / `update` with `--resume` reopens the kept work directory of the key, verifies that the package coordinate, option and chosen features match, and continues from the first step that is not `done`; `--from-step ID` restarts at a named step instead. Without a kept work directory `--resume` is a clear error. A resume never re-fetches an input whose verified file is still in place.

p.failure: A failed step ends the sequence: nothing after it runs, no payload is placed, no root is registered, the index is untouched, and the message names the step, its kind, the work directory and `--resume`. An `optional` step that fails is recorded `failed` and the sequence continues. A failed `finish` step leaves the placed payload or registered root in place and the index written, reports the step, and `uninstall` remains available.

p.record: The index record of an installation keeps the chosen features and the step outcomes (`id`, `kind`, `outcome`), plus the uninstall data recorded by shell and native steps. `uninstall` runs the recorded uninstall commands in reverse step order before deleting an owned payload or leaving an external root; `--force` selects the forced variants as today. `vibe app steps PACKAGE` prints the declared steps and features of a package as written, for editors and agents.

p.describe: `vibe app describe PACKAGE --json` is the one document a graphical tool or an agent needs to build the whole choice: the package identity, every installer option with its platform, architecture, result, portability, launchers and public commands, the option's features with their defaults, and its steps as declared (`vibe-app-describe/1`). It resolves nothing and runs nothing; `plan` is the resolved view for one chosen option and feature set, and `install` consumes the same flags the two documents name. Features are reported with their tree, relations and profiles (`#feature-tree`, `#profiles`).

p.sugar: The method forms map to steps exactly: `zip` / `tar_gz` → one `archive` step; `shell` → one `shell` step with `result = { external }`; `exe` / `msi` → one `native` step with `result = { external }`; `source_build` → one `sources` step then one `recipe` step. A package may switch from `installation` to `steps` without any change in behaviour.

p.feature-tree: Features may form a tree and carry relations, all as data on the `[[installer_options.features]]` row: `parent = "ID"` (any depth, no cycles), `required = true` (cannot be deselected while its parent is selected; a root marked required is always selected), `requires = ["ID", …]` (selecting this feature selects those), and `exclusive_group = "NAME"` (exactly one feature of a group is selected; the group's default is the member whose `default` is true, exactly one per group). Selection is resolved by one deterministic rule set: terminal answers, a profile, retained update choices or defaults supply the base; direct `--feature` / `--no-feature` flags apply on top. Profile and terminal entries are not direct additions that conflict with those flags. Ordinary parent/requires/required implications reach a fixed point before group defaults; all active empty groups choose their fallback from that same closed snapshot, then closure repeats. Declaration and group-name order must not change success or selected membership. Incompatible implications/defaults refuse rather than searching for another user answer. The relation rules are: selecting a feature selects its ancestors and its `requires`; deselecting a feature deselects its descendants; a `required` child of a selected parent and a feature another selected feature requires cannot be deselected and a request to do so is a planning refusal naming the reason; an exclusive group with two direct selections is a refusal, and replacing a base group member must refuse if it would discard another directly selected descendant. The closed set is what conditions see; `describe` reports the tree, the relations and the resolved default set; `plan` reports the resolved set and which features were implied by which rule. A console asks with an indented multi-select; a graphical tool draws the tree.

p.profiles: `[[installer_options.profiles]]` rows (`id`, `name`, optional `description`, `features = [...]`, `default` boolean, at most one default) are named feature sets, the "typical / complete / custom" of classic installers. `--profile ID` selects one and then resolves exactly as explicit choices do; `--feature` / `--no-feature` apply on top of it. Without a profile and without choices the feature defaults apply. An attended terminal offers the profiles first and "custom" opens the tree; a graphical tool does the same on its first page.

p.parameters: `[[installer_options.parameters]]` rows are the typed questions a wizard asks: `id`, `name`, optional `description`, `type` one of `string`, `bool`, `integer`, `choice`, `path`, optional `default`, `required` (default false), for `integer` optional `min` / `max`, for `choice` a `choices` array of `{ value, name }`, for `path` optional `must_exist`. Values arrive as `--set ID=VALUE` (repeatable), from an attended terminal as typed prompts, otherwise from `default`; a required parameter with no value is a planning refusal. Values are validated at planning time against the type, never later. Steps read them as `$param:ID` in templates and recipe/shell receive `VIBE_PARAM_<ID>` (ASCII upper-cased, `-` and `.` to `_`) in the environment; installer declarations using that channel must have distinct, representable emitted keys (PROP-069#APP-ENV-IDENTITY); a condition may test `param = "ID"` (a `bool` true or a non-empty value) or `param_equals = { id = "ID", value = "V" }`. Chosen values are recorded with the installation (never for a parameter marked `secret = true`, which remains an ephemeral recipe/shell execution input and must be omitted from framework-owned views and records; arbitrary package-authored child output/content is not sandboxed by this marking).

p.license: A package may declare `[installer_options.license]` with `file` (package-relative text) and `name`. When present, installation needs explicit acceptance: `--accept-license` on the command line, or a yes in an attended terminal after the text is shown; unattended without the flag is a planning refusal. `describe` reports the file and name; the acceptance is recorded with the installation. Nothing is downloaded before acceptance.

p.sizes: A `sources` input and an `archive` step may declare `size` (bytes) beside `sha256`. The planner sums the sizes of the inputs that will be fetched and reports `download_bytes` with a flag for inputs of unknown size; a cache hit counts zero. The runner reports fetched bytes against the declared size as progress and refuses an input that exceeds its declared size. Every HTTP fetch of an input is a transfer of `spec://org.vibevm.core/vibevm/common/PROP-068#transfer` (purpose `package-source`, `archive` or `native-input`, batch the run's id): its samples are the step's byte measurements, and the journal under the settings root keeps it for any tool on the machine.

p.icon: `[application] icon` names a package-relative image — or the icon set of PROP-059 `#menu` — for the application as a whole (a launcher's `icon` stays the launcher's own). `describe` reports its absolute path in the resolved package tree; at install the file is copied into the home as PROP-059 `#menu` prescribes, and `app list --json` reports that copy when present.

p.runs: Every run of an installation (install, update, resume, uninstall) writes `<home>/cache/app-runs/<key>/<timestamp>/` with `steps.json`, the plan, and one `steps/<id>/output.log` per executed step holding that step's child output (and, for agent steps, the envelope of `PROP-064#envelope`); the work directory's own copy is what resume uses. `vibe app runs PACKAGE [--json]` lists the records newest first with outcome and path; `vibe app runs PACKAGE --prune N` keeps the newest N. A graphical tool shows a run's log from this path; vibe never truncates a log it is writing.

p.work: `install` / `update` (with `-g` and in a project, whose home applies the same request) and `vibe app modify` with `--keep-work` do not delete the work directory of a successful run: the directory and its `steps.json` stay with every step `done`, the human report ends with `work directory kept: <path>` and the JSON report carries `work`. A later run of the same key without `--resume` / `--from-step` replaces that directory and says so first (`replacing kept work directory <path> (<size>)`); `--from-step ID` restarts inside it without re-fetching anything, and `--resume` on a directory whose every step has already run is refused as `nothing_to_resume` naming `--from-step ID`. `vibe app work [PACKAGE] [--json]` lists the kept directories of the selected home (`vibe-app-work/1`): the package key, the state (`failed` or `interrupted` with the step responsible, `delegated`, `done` for a directory kept after success, `unknown` without a readable `steps.json`), the change time of `steps.json`, and the total bytes with the share of `sources/`, `out/`, `inputs/` and the rest; a named package with no kept directory is the refusal `work_missing`. `vibe app work PACKAGE --clean` deletes that one directory and `vibe app work --clean --all` every kept directory of the home, reporting each removal and the bytes freed; `--clean` with neither a package nor `--all` is a usage error. A clean touches nothing outside `<home>/cache/app-work/`: the download cache of `#execution` and the run records of `#runs` survive it, and it is refused while another vibe command holds the home's mutation lock.

p.display: An attended run of `install`, `update` or a project materialisation draws a step panel on stderr: one row per step labelled `<id> (<kind>) <title>`, the rows nested as a tree in the sense of `PROP-060#DISPLAY` — the command's own row the root, each step a child, a required package's whole install a subtree under its own `requires <key> (<scope>) for step <id>` row, and the folded child-output lines under the running step's own vertical — with a spinner and elapsed time while it runs, the renderer's `✓ … [elapsed]` record once it finishes, and its reason once, dimmed, when it is skipped; a download shows a bytes bar against the size `#sizes` declares or the server's `Content-Length`, and the transferred bytes alone when neither is known. The running step's child output does not reach the terminal — the run log of `#runs` still receives every byte — and the last five lines are folded under the step as dim rows, stripped of control characters, bounded to the viewport and refreshed as lines arrive. `l` replaces the fold with the live stream printed above the panel and folds it back; the change takes effect at the next line and no history is redrawn. No other key means anything, and `q` is not one. Keys are read from the terminal in raw mode on a dedicated thread while a non-attached child runs, and the terminal mode is restored on every exit path; a `Ctrl-C` key event delivers the very interrupt the signal handling of `#cancellation` registered — `SIGINT` where raw mode cleared `ISIG`, a `CTRL_C_EVENT` generated for this console's own process group where it cleared `ENABLE_PROCESSED_INPUT` — so the hotkey reads the same on Unix and on Windows and raw mode changes nothing about cancellation. The signal handling is in place before the reader starts. A non-attached child gets no standard input while the panel draws; a child that takes the whole terminal (an interactive agent step of `PROP-064#modes`) stops the key thread, restores the terminal mode and stops the drawing for as long as it runs, as does every question and notice the run itself prints. `--log <auto|live|tail|quiet>` chooses what reaches the terminal — `auto` folds where a terminal can draw a fold and streams live where it cannot, `live` starts with the fold open, `tail` keeps it closed wherever a terminal can draw one and streams live where it cannot, `quiet` shows no child output at all and names each step's log path instead — and `--log-tail N` how many lines the fold keeps (default 5, `0` the step row alone); `VIBE_APP_LOG` and `VIBE_APP_LOG_TAIL` are their fallbacks when neither flag is given. A failing or interrupted step prints the last 30 lines of its log under `last 30 lines of <path>:` after the panel is gone and before the error of `#failure` names the step, the work directory and `--resume`. Redirected output, a dumb terminal, `--quiet`, `--json`, the machine stream of `#events` and the opt-out of `PROP-060#PROGRESS-OPT-OUT` all keep the flat behaviour: plain line records, child output streamed as before, no raw mode and no hotkey. Every attended question of a run — the installer selection, the setup type, the feature tree, each parameter and the license — is drawn with one shared prompt theme built on the renderer's glyphs and its colour decision of `PROP-060#DISPLAY`: `?` before an unanswered question, a cyan `❯` on the row under the cursor, `◉`/`○` on a multi-choice row and the renderer's own `✓` on the answer line, with a blank line above every question and one dim key legend above the first list. A list's rows are aligned columns — the name, the dim id, a green `[detected]` and the description — which keep their alignment and lose only their colour wherever colour is off. How the panel, the questions and their answers look is PROP-067's: a question is a block that collapses to its answer, the running step a block with its fold, the run ends with its trailer (PROP-067 `#question`, `#fold`, `#trailer`). A download is the running block of its step: the bytes and the rate come from the transfer's samples and its own task draws no row (`spec://org.vibevm.core/vibevm/common/PROP-068#stream`, `#display`).

p.cancellation: An interrupted command (Ctrl-C, `SIGTERM`, a console control event, a closed controlling process, or a `Ctrl-C` key event the step panel of `#display` reads in raw mode and re-delivers as the same signal or console control event) stops the running step: the signal is forwarded to the child — on Unix to the child's whole process group, which a captured child that does not read the terminal leads, so a recipe's shell and the compiler or `sleep` it waits on stop together (bash, `/bin/sh` on macOS, otherwise carries on with the script when only the shell is signalled) — vibe waits for it, records the step `interrupted` in `steps.json`, keeps the work directory and exits with the step failure code. The next `--resume` continues from that step. No step is marked `done` by an interrupted exit, and an owned payload is never placed by one.

p.events: `--progress-format json` (global flag, also `VIBE_PROGRESS_FORMAT=json`) makes every progress observation of `PROP-060` a JSON line on stderr (`vibe-progress-event/1`: sequence, timestamp, task id, parent, kind `start` | `measurement` | `detail` | `diagnostic` | `finish` | `skip` | `fail`, label, completed / total / unit when measured, message). Step execution emits one task per step labelled with the step id and title, a `measurement` per fetched input, and the child output as `detail` lines; agent steps emit `start`, consent, delivery and `finish`. `--json` keeps the final envelope on stdout; the two streams never mix. This is the one live channel a graphical tool consumes.

p.error-codes: The JSON error envelope carries `code`: a stable snake_case identifier of the refusal or failure (`not_installed`, `selection_required`, `locked`, `need_unmet`, `plan_refused`, `license_required`, `parameter_invalid`, `step_failed`, `agent_missing`, `consent_required`, `unavailable`, `work_missing`, …) beside the human `error` text, plus `step` when a step is responsible and `work` when a work directory is kept. Human output keeps the text. Codes are the application subsystem's error variants in snake_case and are listed by `vibe app errors --json`.

p.exit-codes: Exit status: `0` success; `1` a step failed or the installation was interrupted (resumable; `work` names where); `2` the request was refused before any effect (usage, planning refusal, unmet need, missing consent or license, invalid parameter, locked); `75` the run is parked for a hosting agent (`PROP-064#parking`). A launcher's or proxy's own exit status passes through unchanged.

p.modify: Every choice a package offers can be changed after installation, the "modify" of classic maintenance mode: another installer option (a source build instead of a binary, another platform package), another feature set, another profile, other parameter values. `vibe app modify PACKAGE [--installer ID] [--profile ID] [--feature …] [--no-feature …] [--set …] [--accept-license]` takes the installed record, plans the new choice against the same package version (anything not named keeps its recorded value), shows what the old choice recorded as uninstall data and what the new plan will run, then runs the recorded uninstall commands of the old steps in reverse order, installs the new choice through the ordinary engine, and rewrites the record while keeping the slot, its default and its public commands. An owned payload of the old choice is deleted after the new one is placed. In an attended terminal without flags it asks the wizard's questions with the recorded values preselected; a graphical tool drives it with the same flags it uses for `install`. `update -g` keeps following whatever the record says. `install -g --force` is "repair" and `uninstall -g` is "remove" of the same vocabulary.

p.outdated: `vibe app outdated [--json]` reports, for every installed application, its installed version and the newest version the configured registries offer for the same package (`vibe-app-outdated/1`), without changing anything; `--offline` answers from the registry cache only. `update -g` is the action; no automatic or scheduled update exists in vibe, a graphical tool or a scheduler polls `outdated` and calls `update`.

p.env-step: `kind = "env"` changes the user's durable environment declaratively, the Environment table of classic installers: `set = { NAME = "template" }`, `unset = ["NAME"]`, `path_prepend = ["template", …]`, always `phase = "finish"` (values may name `$app_root`, `$app_bin`, `$vibe_home`). Scope is the current user only; the system environment is never touched and PATH is only ever edited through `path_prepend`. On Windows the step edits `HKCU\Environment` reading `REG_EXPAND_SZ` values raw and writing them back with their kind preserved, then broadcasts the environment change, all through the registry API and `SendMessageTimeoutW` with no child process (PROP-019 `#path`). On Linux and macOS vibe owns `<settings>/env.sh` (and `env.fish`) holding one line per entry tagged with the installation key, and exactly one managed block (`spec://org.vibevm.world/managed-blocks/flows/managed-blocks/MANAGED-BLOCKS-PROTOCOL#root`) in the user's `~/.profile`, `~/.bashrc`, `~/.zshrc` and fish config that sources that file; the block is written on first use and removed when no entry remains, and no byte outside it is ever touched. On Windows, removing vibe's last entry from a `Path` value that vibe itself created deletes the value; a value that existed before (even empty) is written back exactly as it was, with its kind. The applied entries are recorded with the installation so `uninstall` and `modify` remove exactly them; `app list --json` reports them. A new shell sees the change; `vibe shell` applies the recorded entries of installed applications immediately. Configuration files are placed with `copy` in the `finish` phase; an arbitrary script stays an honest `shell` step.

p.app-dependencies: An installer option or a single step may name other application packages it requires: `requires = ["<group>/<name>@<req>", …]`, the same `group/name@requirement` spelling the package manifest's `[requires]` table uses. A step-level `requires` is an optional dependency in the only sense that matters: it is needed exactly when that step runs. Requirements are resolved by the ordinary vibe dependency resolver (PROP-001 / PROP-008): across every configured registry in their order, by version requirement, through the same index, mirror and offline rules every other package kind obeys — never by URL, never bound to one hosting service. The planner first consults the home's index (an installed version satisfying the requirement is used as is), otherwise the resolver, and shows the result as a `dependency` entry of the plan ahead of the step that needs it; `install` installs it through the ordinary engine, in the same home and under the same consent, before continuing. In a project, a required application is recorded in `vibe.lock` like any other transitive dependency, and the project home materialises it from that record. A requirement has a scope. The default for a step-level requirement is `build`: the required package is installed hidden (PROP-059 `#hidden-installations`: payload, index record, movable and removable, but no proxy, no alternative, never a default), so installing Vim from sources leaves nothing on the user's PATH but Vim. Several versions of such a toolchain coexist as separate installations of one slot, each matched to the requirement that asked for it. The user reaches it as any hidden installation: `vibe shell --with` for one session, `vibe app expose` permanently. A requirement with `scope = "runtime"` (an interpreter or runtime the launchers need) is installed exposed. `app list` shows hidden installations in their own section with what requires them. While a step runs, the `bin` directory of every required owned installation and the public commands of every required installation are prepended to the child's PATH, so a `needs = ["command:gcc"]` is met by a `mingw-w64` package as well as by the host. Requirements are recorded with the installation; `app list --json` names what each installation requires and what requires it. The task under which a requirement installs starts with a structured `requires` member on the machine progress stream (`spec://org.vibevm.core/vibevm/common/PROP-060#MACHINE-STREAM`) beside its unchanged label. Removal of a tree is `#uninstall-tree`.

p.uninstall-tree: Every installation carries a mark: `manual` when the user asked for it by name (`install`, `expose`, or `app mark manual`), `auto` when a requirement pulled it in, with the installations that required it recorded. `vibe uninstall -g PKG` removes exactly PKG. Auto installations that nothing requires any more are not removed silently: the command lists them as orphans, `--autoremove` on the same command or a separate `vibe app autoremove` removes them, and a manual installation is never removed by autoremove. An installation that another installation requires at runtime scope blocks its own removal: the command refuses and names the dependents; `--cascade` removes the dependents too after showing the plan. A build-scope requirement holds nothing after the build and may always be removed; the requirement stays recorded, and a later `modify` or reinstall pulls it in again. `--plan-only` shows the removal as a plan in the install plan's shape: dependents before dependencies, `finish` steps' removal before `prepare` steps', and for each installation its authored removal first (a shell step's `uninstall` command, an env step's rollback), then proxies and alternatives, then the owned payload, then the index record. Removal never touches files outside the payload and the step results — configuration an application wrote under the user's home stays. A removal writes the same run record as an installation. In a project, deleting the dependency row leads to the same removal in the project home, orphans included.

p.update-and-rollback: `vibe app update PKG` installs the newer version as a new installation key and moves the slot's default and the public commands to it; the previous installation is not removed but kept hidden (PROP-059 `#hidden-installations`) until the next successful update of the same slot removes it, so a source build taking minutes is never thrown away by an update that turns out worse. `vibe app rollback PKG` exposes the kept previous installation, makes it the default again and hides the newer one; `--purge-previous` on update, or `vibe app autoremove`, removes kept previous versions at once. An installation may be held: `vibe app hold PKG` / `vibe app unhold PKG` set a `held` flag in its index record; `outdated` reports a held installation as held, a bulk `update` skips it, and only `update PKG` naming it explicitly moves it. The record of an update names the key it replaced.

p.ordinary-reach: **Owner decision 2026-11-10 — structured, multi-step installation reaches ordinary packages, and it does so through the mechanism that already exists rather than through a second one.** The owner's requirement is that a project or library package be able to do what only an application can do today: run several named things after it is installed, in order, with its prerequisites checked first and its outcome visible. The answer is **not** to admit `[[installer_options]]` on another kind. That refusal stays exactly as it is (`[[installer_options]] requires [application] identity` and `… requires [package] kind = app`, `crates/vibe-core/src/manifest/document/validation.rs`), and this fact records its reason so nobody re-opens it: an installer option is a **per-platform alternative that produces a payload** — it carries `platform`, `arch`, `result`, `path_dirs`, launchers and public commands, and its steps write `$VIBE_OUT`, which becomes an owned payload under a slot's library. An ordinary package has no payload, no slot, no app root and no platform alternatives: it has a materialised slot in `vibedeps/` that **is** its content. Admitting the table would import that whole vocabulary as fields every ordinary package must leave empty, which is how a grammar rots. **The declaration for an ordinary package is PROP-054's `[[extension]]` at the two `slot:` points** — `slot:pre-install` and `slot:post-install` (`spec://org.vibevm.core/vibevm/common/PROP-054#POINT-GRAMMAR`) — which is already the general, multiple-contributions-per-point form of exactly this act, is already implemented (`crates/vibe-core/src/manifest/extension.rs`, `crates/vibe-core/src/lifecycle/point.rs`, `crates/vibe-extension-registry/src/collect.rs`), already carries an `id` per contribution, a handler taxonomy, host activation and disabling (`[[extensions.use]]`, `[extensions] disable`), and is already what `[hooks]` lowers into (`crates/vibe-install/src/lifecycle/plan.rs` builds a synthetic `ExtensionDecl { point: Slot(…), handler: Script { base } }` from `[hooks] pre-install` / `post-install`). So PROP-020's single hooks stay the one-contribution short spelling of a list, exactly as `#purpose` already says the single-method form of `PROP-059#installer-separation` is the short spelling of a one-step list — the same sentence, one plane over. **No third mechanism is created.** PROP-054 `#REJ-TWO-GRAMMARS` names a second extension grammar as the failure mode, and a package-scope step table beside `[[extension]]` would have been exactly that.

p.ordinary-grammar: **Decided 2026-11-10 — what a `slot:` contribution gains from this document, and what it does not.** The `slot:` plane keeps PROP-054's own handler taxonomy for *what runs* (`builtin`, `script`, `binary`, `native`, `agent` — `#HANDLER-KINDS`), and this document's step **kinds** stay the application plane's vocabulary. The two are deliberately not merged: `archive`, `sources`, `copy` and `env` exist to produce or place a payload and to change a user's durable environment from an app root, and neither notion exists on the lifecycle plane. **What is shared is everything that decides whether, and in what order, something runs, and how it is seen** — which is the half an ordinary package is actually missing. A `slot:` contribution therefore gains exactly four fields, each with the meaning it has here and no other: `title`, the human line (`#steps`), so a plan and a panel have something to print beside an `id`; `when` / `unless`, taking **this document's closed condition vocabulary** (`#conditions`) — `feature`, `param`, `param_equals`, `command_present`, `file_present`, `env_present`, `agent_configured`, `offline` — where `feature` and `param` read the **package-scope** configuration PROP-069 `#AUTHORED-DEFINITIONS` already admits for every one of the nine kinds, which is what makes the condition evaluable without an application's installer option; `needs` (`#needs`), checked for every contribution that will run **before anything starts**, refusing the package's installation up front and naming the contribution and the missing need, which is the single most valuable field an ordinary package is missing today; and `optional` (`#steps`), whose unmet need or failure is recorded and does not stop the rest. Nothing else crosses: a `slot:` contribution that names `requires` (the application dependencies of `#app-dependencies`), `phase`, `result`, or a template variable of `$out`, `$sources`, `$app_root` or `$app_bin` is a **validation refusal naming the field**, not a silently ignored declaration — the precedent is PROP-075 `#P6-AS-BUILT`'s second amendment, where a migration step's four inapplicable fields are refused for the same reason. `phase` is refused because the point already *is* the phase: `slot:pre-install` is this document's `prepare` and `slot:post-install` is its `finish`, which is why no new vocabulary is introduced for ordering across the two moments. `requires` is refused because installing an application from inside an ordinary package's materialisation is a second install plane this decision does not open; the honest alternative is `needs = ["command:NAME"]`, which refuses up front and names what is missing, and that is what B-188 needs.

p.ordinary-plan: **Decided 2026-11-10 — the plan, the panel, the logs, and the one library both planes share.** The judgment half named in `#ordinary-grammar` is **one library used by both planes**, not a second implementation: the condition evaluator, the needs preflight and the plan projection take declared rows plus host facts and return `run` / `skip (reason)` / `refuse (missing need)`, with no filesystem mutation, no process start and no prompt — the shape PROP-069 `#PURE-CORE` already requires of shared configuration logic. **Execution is not shared, and that is deliberate**: an ordinary package's contributions are run by the lifecycle handler engine that `[hooks]` already runs through (`crates/vibe-install/src/lifecycle.rs`), never by the application step runner (`crates/vibe-app/src/steps/run.rs`), because that runner is keyed to an installation key, a library, a payload root and `$VIBE_OUT`, of which an ordinary package has none — reusing it would have meant inventing all four for a package that needs none of them. **What the user sees.** `vibe install --plan-only` and `vibe install` print the selected `slot:` contributions of every package the run will materialise, as a subtree under that package, in the shape `#plan` already draws — one row per contribution with its `id`, its handler kind, its `title`, its needs and its `run` / `skip (reason)` verdict — and an attended run draws them in the step panel of `#display`, one row per contribution, with the running contribution's child output kept off the terminal and every byte written to its own log. The evidence is one directory per package version, `<home>/cache/install-steps/<group>/<name>/<version>/<timestamp>/`, holding `steps.json` (`vibe-install-steps/1`: per contribution the `id`, handler kind, outcome, reason, start and finish times) and `logs/<id>.log`; vibe never truncates a log it is writing, as `#runs` already states. The install report — human and JSON — carries the same rows per package, which is what makes a skipped or failed contribution visible to a client and not only to a person. The directory is derived state: it is listed and cleaned by the ordinary cache surface and nothing resumes from it. **The evidence record and the panel landed 2026-11-10 (the P7e tail), and one residue keeps this fact `impl/work`.** `vibe-install-steps/1` is a registered format (`schemas/install_steps.jtd.json`, `[format.install-steps]`, a generated reader, an authored corpus under `formats/corpora/install-steps/e1/`), and a run writes one record directory per package version — `steps.json` rewritten as each contribution ends, so a run that is killed leaves the rows it had reached, and `logs/<id>.log` beside it. Each row carries the author's own `id` (not the engine's execution key, which is carried too), the point, the handler kind, the outcome in the engine's own words, the reason a skip or a failure gives, and the instants it started and finished — the start taken at a new observer seam, because the engine that runs contributions is handed no clock. The evidence is **derived state that may never fail an install**: an unresolvable settings home, a read-only cache or a full disk costs the record and not the work, which is why that cell ends every path in a discarded result. The **panel** is one row per running contribution on the shared renderer, labelled `<id> (<kind>) <title>` as `#display` prescribes, with the flat line records kept exactly where a terminal cannot draw one (`--json`, `--quiet`, the machine stream, redirected output) rather than printed beside it. **The residue, named rather than implied:** an attended run still streams a contribution's child output to the terminal, so there are no captured bytes to write and such a row carries no log; and a captured row's log holds the first mebibyte of each stream, with `logTruncated` saying so. Both follow from the engine's stream handling — `StreamMode::Inherit` gives vibe no bytes at all, and `read_capped` bounds what a capture hands back — so closing them is a change in `vibe-lifecycle`'s process layer (a log sink the engine writes as the bytes arrive), together with the `--log`/`--log-tail` fold `#display` describes. That is this fact's remaining work and nobody else's.

p.ordinary-failure: **Decided 2026-11-10 — failure, interruption and retry keep PROP-020's law, not this document's.** An ordinary package's installation already has a failure contract and it is the one that holds: a failing `slot:pre-install` contribution **aborts that package's installation and the materialised slot is rolled back**, nothing is registered, projected or written for it, and the failing package is named (PROP-020 `#FAIL-PRE-ABORTS`); a failing `slot:post-install` contribution leaves the package **installed and flagged**, with a warning carrying the contribution id, its captured output and its log path, and never a silent success (`#FAIL-POST-FLAGS`). That is kept rather than replaced by this document's `#failure` because the two differ on purpose — an application's `prepare` failure has a payload staged in a work directory and nothing placed, while an ordinary package's slot is already populated and *is* the thing to undo — and changing it would be a behaviour break for every package that declares `[hooks]` today. Within one point, a failing contribution ends that point's sequence for that package: nothing after it runs, and an `optional` one is recorded `failed` and the sequence continues, as `#failure` says for a step. **The stop law is this document's, unchanged** (`#cancellation`): an interrupt stops the running contribution, the signal reaches the child and its process group, the outcome is recorded `interrupted`, **no contribution is marked `done` by an interrupted exit, and nothing after it runs** — and for a `pre-install` interrupt the slot is rolled back exactly as for a failure, so an interrupted install never leaves a package half-registered. **Retry is a rerun, not a resume.** There is no `--resume` and no `--from-step` on this plane, because both need a kept work directory keyed to an installation key an ordinary package does not have; the retry is `vibe reinstall <group>/<name>`, which restores the recorded payload and so makes PROP-020 `#RESET-THEN-RERUN`'s payload diff non-empty, which is the condition under which contributions rerun. The failure message names that exact command. PROP-020 `#RESET-THEN-RERUN`'s standing warning stands with it: contributions must be idempotent until a hook-output ownership contract exists, and a rerun may compound state they created outside the recorded payload. **Implemented 2026-11-10 (the P7e tail), as one classifier and three corrections.** The law is a pure function of the three facts the dispatcher already holds — was a stop requested, is this PROP-020 `#FAIL-POST-FLAGS`' soft post-install case, is the contribution `optional` (`crates/vibe-install/src/lifecycle/failure.rs`) — so it is tested as a table rather than inferred from three failing installs. **(1) The retry is in the message**, the same sentence in both channels, the row a client reads and the error the run refuses with: it names `vibe reinstall <group>/<name>` and says that it is a rerun and that this plane has no `--resume` and no `--from-step`. A host-declared row, which no reinstall of a dependency reruns, is given no command rather than a wrong one. **(2) An `optional` contribution's failure is recorded `fail` and flagged and the point's sequence continues** — before this it aborted the installation exactly as a required one did, so `optional = true` meant nothing once the contribution actually ran. Flagged rather than bare, because a failure the run goes on past must never read as a silent success. **(3) A failure under a requested stop is recorded `interrupted`, flags nothing, and stops even when the contribution is `optional`**, read from the pass's own cancellation token rather than guessed from a message; the signal reaching the child and its process group is the controlled runner's, unchanged, and a `pre-install` interrupt rolls the slot back by the path a failure already takes. The post-install warning's **log path** is the evidence record of `#ordinary-plan`, written beside the row, and — as this clause already says — it is the *captured* output that is carried, so a run whose child wrote straight to the terminal has none. `[hooks]` keeps the behaviour it has: a one-field hook declares no `optional`, so its failures classify exactly as before. Offline tests: `crates/vibe-install/tests/slot_failure_law.rs` dispatches real rows for all three outcomes, `failure.rs`'s own table test pins the classifier, and the whole `[hooks]` suite runs unchanged.

p.ordinary-consumer: **Decided 2026-11-10 — the first consumer, and the boundary of the decision.** The consumer is `B-188`: installing `org.vibevm.ai-native/rust-ai-native` copies source and stops, leaving the reader to discover `vibe bin build` and `vibe mcp install` and four unnamed prerequisites (`rustfmt`, `clippy`, `cargo-nextest`, `rust-analyzer`), none of which is checked before a gate fails. Expressed here it is two `slot:post-install` contributions with `title`s, `needs = ["command:cargo", "command:rustfmt", "command:clippy", "command:cargo-nextest"]` on the one that builds, and `optional = true` on the one that would write into the user's agents — so the prerequisites are named and refused **up front** instead of surfacing as a failed gate, the two acts appear in `--plan-only` before anything runs, and each has its own log. That is the whole of B-188's first half, and it is the acceptance this decision is measured by. **Out of scope, named so nobody assumes it**: no new extension point (the `slot:` family stays `pre-install` and `post-install`, and PROP-054 `#REJ-FULL-MAVEN-PHASES` keeps the point namespace closed behind a ruling); no package-declared user-invokable verb (a `[[command]]` is host-only by PROP-054 `#HOST-RUN-COMMANDS`, deliberately, so that installing a dependency cannot inject an ambient script, and this decision does not weaken it); no payload, `$out` or `result` on the ordinary plane; no sandboxing (PROP-020 `#OOS-SANDBOXING` stands — contributions run with the user's privileges and that is the accepted posture, not an oversight); and no change to the project plane's existing arbitrary-code consent gate, which is what already makes materialising a dependency's installers a decision the user takes.

p.ordinary-trust:
**Owner decision 2026-11-10 — a dependency's contributions run unasked only from a trusted group, and the allow-list is one that already exists.** A `slot:` contribution declared by a project **dependency** is package-authored code that acts with the user's authority at materialisation time, exactly as an agent step's prompt is, so it is gated by the allow-lists vibe already has and by no new one. The trusted set for an authored `[[extension]]` row at a `slot:` point is the `trusted_groups` array of `<settings>/agents.toml` (`spec://org.vibevm.core/vibevm/common/PROP-064#consent`, the mechanism `vibe agent list` prints and the exact-string group match it already uses) **unioned with PROP-020's default hook allow-list** (`#trust-gate`'s `DEFAULT_ALLOWED_GROUPS`, which is `org.vibevm`). The union is required rather than convenient: `[hooks]` is the one-contribution short spelling of exactly this row (`#ordinary-reach`), so a group already trusted to run a hook must be trusted to run the same act written in the long form — otherwise the sugar would be more privileged than the grammar it lowers into. Neither existing list is widened by this: the agent gate reads the agent list as before, and the hook list is read, not changed. A contribution declared by the **host's own manifest** asks nothing, because a project's own `vibe.toml` is the user's own word — the same reason `[[command]]` is host-only (PROP-054 `#HOST-RUN-COMMANDS`). For an untrusted dependency the verdicts are PROP-020 `#trust-gate`'s, unchanged: an **attended** install asks **once per package**, listing every contribution that will run with its `id`, its handler kind and its `title`, and a decline is a refusal that runs nothing; an **unattended** install refuses **before the first contribution starts**, naming the package, its group, and the two remedies — add the group to `trusted_groups` in `<settings>/agents.toml`, or rerun with `--assume-yes` (which `--unattended` implies) or `--allow-hooks`. **No flag is invented**: the per-run escapes are the two that already exist for these two lists. The question is asked only when at least one contribution of that package **will actually run** after its conditions (`#ordinary-grammar`) and its `needs` preflight, so a package all of whose contributions skip asks nothing, and a repeat install whose payload diff is empty (PROP-020 `#RESET-THEN-RERUN`) asks nothing because nothing reruns. **Plain `[hooks]` keeps exactly the behaviour it has, and that is the compatibility rule — stated against what the code does rather than against what PROP-020 says.** Measured while implementing this: on the canonical install path `[hooks]` is lowered to a synthetic `slot:` script contribution and run through the lifecycle handler engine, which consults **no** `HookPolicy` and asks nothing — `crates/vibe-install/src/apply.rs` says so in as many words, «install itself is consent, so this path has no `HookPolicy` or prompt surface», and nothing in `vibe-cli` ever constructs one. PROP-020 `#trust-gate`'s allow-list, consent question and unattended refusal are therefore reached only by the legacy `apply` entry points, which no command uses. So the two gates are **not** behaviourally identical today, and gating `[hooks]` here would newly ask — or, unattended, newly refuse — for every published package that declares one. It is left exactly as it is: a `[hooks]` entry runs unasked, because materialising a dependency at all is the consent the project plane already takes (`#ordinary-consumer`). Only an authored `[[extension]]` row at a `slot:` point is gated here, which no published package carries yet, so this decision breaks nothing and tightens only the grammar it comes with. The residue is recorded rather than removed: PROP-020 `#trust-gate` is unreached on the path every command takes, which is a defect of that gate and not of this one; closing it is a later decision with its own migration, not a silent widening or tightening taken here (`BACKLOG.md#b-258`).
**Amendment, owner decision 2026-11-10 — the two allow-lists are now ONE, everything under `org.vibevm.*` is trusted by default, and `untrusted_groups` is how that trust is refused.** Verbatim: «Доверять по умолчанию всему org.vibevm.*, и сделать этот механизм конфигурируемым (базовые trusted_groups для vibevm, которые у пользователя эффективно конкатенируются с содержимым его agents.toml)», and, the same day, «я бы сделал еще механизм недоверенных групп в agents.toml, чтобы можно было запретить доверять встроенному». The union this fact described above is therefore **gone**, and with it the divergence it papered over: there is one mechanism, `vibe_core::trust`, whose grammar, three layers (`base` ++ `site` ++ `user`), deny-wins rule and refusals are `spec://org.vibevm.core/vibevm/common/PROP-064#trust-entries`, and this plane reads the value it resolves. What changes for a dependency's `slot:` contribution, in three sentences. The trusted set is no longer «`trusted_groups` unioned with PROP-020's hook list» but the one effective policy, whose base entry is the **subtree** `org.vibevm.*` — so a dependency in `org.vibevm.ai-native` or `org.vibevm.node` now runs its authored contributions unasked, where before only the exact group `org.vibevm` did, and a package in `org.example` is refused exactly as it was. PROP-020 `#trust-gate`'s `DEFAULT_ALLOWED_GROUPS` no longer exists as a second constant: `vibe-workspace`'s hook gate reads the same base list through the same policy, so the two can no longer disagree whatever either document later says. And the deny list is the one way to take trust back — `untrusted_groups = ["org.vibevm.ai-native"]` in `<settings>/agents.toml` restores the attended question and the unattended refusal for that group while leaving the rest of the subtree trusted, `untrusted_groups = ["org.vibevm.*"]` refuses the built-in trust whole, and an administrator writes either one for a whole installation in the site profile's `[trust]` table. The compatibility rule is unchanged and was re-measured, not re-argued: plain `[hooks]` still runs unasked on the canonical path, because that path still consults no `HookPolicy` — the base list widening is therefore invisible to every published package that declares one, and B-258 stays open with its own migration rather than being closed as a side effect of this amendment.

p.acceptance: Public Linux fixtures: a four-step owned option (`sources` → optional `agent` under `when = { feature }` → `recipe` → `copy`) with `plan` showing run / skip, an unmet `command:` need refused before download, a failing middle step keeping the work directory and `--resume` finishing without re-fetching, `--from-step`, features chosen by flag and by default, a `finish` step seeing `VIBE_APP_ROOT`, uninstall running recorded shell uninstalls in reverse; every existing method fixture unchanged through the sugar mapping. One more fixture covers `#display`: a `--log quiet` install prints no child output and names each step's log, whose file holds every line; a failing step prints the last 30 lines of that log before the error; `--log-tail 0` is accepted and an unnamed `--log` value is refused by the argument parser; the fold, its replacement by the live stream and the bytes bar with a known total are proven against an in-memory terminal, since no step panel is driven from a pseudo-terminal. One more fixture covers `#work`: an install with `--keep-work` leaves the work directory listed by `vibe app work --json` as `done` with a non-zero size, `--from-step build --keep-work` reruns only from that step inside it without fetching again, `vibe app work PACKAGE --clean` removes it, and a package with no kept directory answers `work_missing`. The Vim bridge and the documentation site are rewritten as step lists and installed on this host.

p.launcher-command: A launcher's `executable` may name a command instead of a file in the installed payload: `executable = "command:NAME"`, the spelling `needs = ["command:NAME"]` already uses. `NAME` is a bare command name — no directory separator, no template variable, no whitespace, no control character — and neither the template grammar nor the containment rule of `PROP-059#launcher-paths` applies to it, because none of it is a path; a manifest that spells anything else after `command:` is refused at validation. It is resolved when the launcher runs and never at install time: the entries of `PATH` in order, on Windows the name as it stands when it already ends in a listed `PATHEXT` extension and otherwise the name with each of them appended and never on its own (`.COM;.EXE;.BAT;.CMD` when the environment carries none), because Windows cannot start an extensionless file and a payload directory on PATH may hold one, the first executable file winning, with the running proxy's own image the one file never chosen — so a proxy for `NAME` whose launcher runs `NAME` cannot re-enter itself. Nothing else in that directory is skipped: every installed application's proxy shares it, and a runtime a user installed by name is reached through exactly those. An absent command is not an installation failure. `plan` carries a warning naming the launcher and the command and installs anyway, so a package whose interpreter the machine already carries needs neither a bundled copy nor a dependency; the launch itself fails with one line naming the command, the launcher and how to supply it, and exit `127`. `app launchers` resolves such a launcher like any other — `available` with the found file as its resolved executable, `unavailable: command `NAME` is not on PATH` when there is none — and reports `base` as `path` rather than `app_root`; `describe` and `app installers` report the `command:NAME` spelling unchanged. A package using this form declares `min_vibe_version = "1.0.12"`. This is a third launch form beside a payload file and a derived desktop entry, not a shell, not a search for an interpreter by version, and not a dependency: a package that must have one exact runtime names it with `#app-dependencies` instead, and a package that merely needs an interpreter the user supplies names the command.

p.decisions: Decision: features separate from steps, conditions as data, a closed kind set, a planner, a kept work directory and a resume point. Why: MSI's features / actions / conditions and Inno's uninstall-run tables are the parts of classic installers that survived thirty years; their custom actions and condition expression strings are the parts that did not. Rejected: a transactional engine with rollback (the October prototype), an expression language for conditions (unvalidatable, unrenderable), steps that spawn steps. Revisit when a real package cannot be expressed in the closed vocabulary; add a kind or a condition then, never an escape to scripting the installer.

p.changelog: 2026-11-10 (owner decision, APP-VERSIONS P7e): structured multi-step installation reaches **ordinary** packages, through PROP-054's `[[extension]]` at `slot:pre-install` / `slot:post-install` rather than through a second grammar or a widened `[[installer_options]]`, whose app-only refusal stays with its reason now recorded. Five new facts, all `spec/plan`: `#ordinary-reach` (the decision and why the refusal stays), `#ordinary-grammar` (the four fields a `slot:` contribution gains — `title`, `when` / `unless` over this document's closed condition vocabulary against PROP-069's package-scope configuration, `needs`, `optional` — and the fields it refuses by name), `#ordinary-plan` (one shared judgment library, two execution engines, the plan, the panel, the per-contribution logs and the `vibe-install-steps/1` evidence directory), `#ordinary-failure` (PROP-020's abort-and-roll-back / installed-and-flagged law kept, this document's stop law unchanged, rerun rather than resume) and `#ordinary-consumer` (B-188 as the acceptance, and what stays out). Nothing of the application plane changes. 2026-11-10 (owner decision, the trust amendment): `#ordinary-trust` amended — the two allow-lists it used to union are one mechanism (`vibe_core::trust`,
